title: What Mentally Strong Teachers DON'T Do
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Building on psychoanalyst Amy Morin's "13 Things Mentally Strong People Don't Do" framework, Stuart translates each of her non-examples into a teacher-specific version, covering everything from not wasting energy on uncontrollable circumstances to not resenting colleagues' success to not expecting immediate results from teaching. He treats "mentally weak" and "mentally strong" as descriptive rather than judgmental categories, and repeatedly grounds the abstract principles in his own classroom experience -- jealousy of a colleague's Pinterest-worthy room, anxiety about AI-driven change, past teaching failures. The piece closes by distinguishing mental strength from both intelligence and perfection, arguing it's a set of habits of thought and action rather than a fixed trait. Overall it functions as a wellbeing and professional-identity piece aimed at helping teachers reframe daily frustrations as opportunities rather than personal failures.
points: Stuart reframes each of Morin's 13 "don'ts" through a teacher-specific lens, turning a general self-help framework into a targeted burnout-prevention tool for educators.
His clarification that "mentally weak" isn't an insult and "mentally strong" isn't a compliment -- it's descriptive -- lowers the stakes of self-assessment and makes the list usable without shame.
He models vulnerability by naming his own struggles (jealousy of colleagues, anxiety about AI, past failures) rather than presenting the 13 points as things he's already mastered.
The closing distinction -- mental strength is neither intelligence nor perfection but a buildable habit -- gives teachers a growth-oriented frame instead of a fixed-trait one.
quotes: According to Morin, mentally strong people don't sit around saying, "Why me?" Instead, they focus on what they can do. They acknowledge the challenges and ask, "What's my next best step?
Mentally strong people don't let external circumstances dictate their emotional state. They choose to control their responses. They think, "That comment hurt, but I'll decide how to handle it.

In a world where artificial (AKA contrived, fake) "intelligence" challenges the very idea that helping students grow smarter and mentally stronger is necessary, boy is education ever in a time of flux.

It's tempting to feel underappreciated as a teacher — and you and I probably are. But mentally strong teachers don't wait for praise, raises, or recognition. Heck — the strongest ones don't even expect these things.

You may not see the impact of your teaching today or tomorrow — but that doesn't mean it's not happening. Mentally strong teachers trust that their daily efforts — the lessons, the encouragement, the accountability — are planting seeds that will grow over time.
Nope — this is all about building habits of thought and action that help us handle challenges without burning out. Every day, we get to choose how we respond to the pressures of our work.
